t: The ancestors of the Māori sailed from eastern Polynesia in ocean-going waka and settled New Zealand around 1250–1350, last of all the Polynesian lands.
In isolation they built a distinct culture: the moa-hunting Archaic period gave way after 1500 to the Classic culture of iwi and hapū, pounamu, carved meeting houses and fortified pā.
After European contact Māori traded and adopted new tools and writing, but suffered war, disease and the loss of most of their land; today they lead a strong revival of their language and culture.
dyk: When missionaries met Māori in 1815, Māori could draw accurate maps of their tribal boundaries on paper that matched European maps; the missionaries guessed that they had traditionally drawn maps on sand.
ev: Polynesian settlers arrive in New Zealand in ocean-going waka, the main settlement coming in the first half of the 14th century
A group of Māori settles the Chatham Islands (Rēkohu) and becomes the Moriori
A significantly cooler climate and the extinction of the moa help bring about the Classic Māori culture
Abel Tasman reaches New Zealand; a skirmish leaves four of his men and at least one Māori dead
James Cook’s first voyage brings the first lasting contact between Māori and Europeans
The Musket Wars between iwi kill many and drive others from their lands
The Treaty of Waitangi is first signed at Waitangi by the British Crown and Māori chiefs

f.homeland: New Zealand (Aotearoa), above all the North Island; the Archaic site of Wairau Bar in the South Island, Otago and the mouth of the Waitaki River; Waitangi; the Chatham Islands (Rēkohu), home of the related Moriori.
f.period: Settlement c. 1250–1350; Archaic period c. 1300–1500; Classic period c. 1500–1769; early European contact 1769–1840; the Treaty of Waitangi, 1840; a living people today.
f.known: voyaging waka and whakapapa (genealogy); iwi, hapū and whānau; tapu, noa and mana; pounamu (greenstone) weapons and ornaments; carved war canoes and wharenui (meeting houses); fortified pā; the haka; the Treaty of Waitangi
f.sources: Archaeology (Wairau Bar, moa-hunting sites, pā); radiocarbon dating and the Kaharoa Tephra; DNA and language studies; Māori oral history and genealogies; the journals of James Cook and other European visitors.
